Tidal turbines feed a village for a winter

By Marit Halvorsen, 14 November 2025

For five months the village of Carradale drew most of its electricity from the water moving past its own harbour wall. A five-turbine array anchored in the Kilbrannan Sound delivered 1.4 gigawatt-hours between June and November, enough to carry 340 households plus the fish-processing shed that is the village's largest single load.

The turbines are unremarkable machines. Each one is a three-bladed rotor eighteen metres across, bolted to a gravity base that was floated out and sunk in a single tide window. What is new is the scheduling: because tidal flow is predictable years ahead, the operator sold the output as firm capacity rather than as intermittent generation, and was paid accordingly.

"We know to the minute what we will produce next March," said the array's operations manager. "Nobody can say that about a wind farm." That predictability is the argument the industry has been making for two decades, and Carradale is the first place in Scotland where a grid operator has priced it in.

The costs remain stubborn. At roughly £240 per megawatt-hour the array is far more expensive than the offshore wind now being built in the North Sea, and the project only closed because a research grant covered the gravity bases. Whether the next array is built without one is the question the sector will answer over the coming two years.
